figures.caption: Figure 1: Any3R is a feed-forward model that reconstructs a scene and its camera poses from views of any mix of central cameras.

Figure 2: Motivation. Read from the pixel grid (ii), a patch position stands for a different direction and a pixel for a different solid angle on every lens (i), and the ray field (iii) corrects both. In the bottom row the ray field is withheld, so the backbone reads every frame as a panorama and the reconstruction follows that reading, which is correct only at 360∘360^{\circ}.

Figure 3: Overview. The ray field 𝑹\bm{R} of each view gives its patches angular coordinates for the rotary encoding in intra-frame attention, and the heads predict the camera poses and a radial distance dd per pixel, decoded as 𝑿=d​𝑹\bm{X}=d\bm{R}. In training, the point loss ℒpt\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pt}} compares 𝑿\bm{X} with the ground truth 𝑿gt\bm{X}^{\mathrm{gt}}, and the solid angle d​Ω\mathrm{d}\Omega of the same 𝑹\bm{R} weighs the error of each pixel, shown here on the panorama, where cells of equal pixel count cover unequal areas of the sphere.

Figure 8: Projection of the thirteen camera models of Tab. 16. Left of each pair, a section through the camera centre OO shows probe rays spaced 15∘15^{\circ} apart in incidence angle θ\theta, and 30∘30^{\circ} apart for ERP, one colour per angle. Each travels from the scene to OO (solid) and on to its image point (dashed) on the image plane, a focal length ff behind OO, so the spacing of the dots is the model’s r⁡(θ)r(\theta). ERP and ERP-Crop are seen from above, their image being the sphere of radius ff unrolled, and Cylindrical from the side, its image the cylinder wall a distance ff in front. Right of each pair, the same probes in 3D, from their image points through OO to the unit sphere, with the image’s rows and columns drawn on the sphere in grey. Here ϕ\phi and λ\lambda are azimuth and elevation, uu and vv image coordinates, ρ=tan⁡θ\rho=\tan\theta and d=sin2⁡θ+(ξ+cos⁡θ)2d=\sqrt{\sin^{2}\theta+(\xi+\cos\theta)^{2}}. Every camera is built as in the benchmark, with the declared field of view reaching half the image height, k1=−0.18k_{1}=-0.18 and k2=0.02k_{2}=0.02 for Brown–Conrady together with the tangential terms p1=8×10−4p_{1}=8\times 10^{-4} and p2=−6×10−4p_{2}=-6\times 10^{-4}, ω=0.9\omega=0.9 for FOV/ATAN, ξ=1.6\xi=1.6 for MEI, (k1,k2,k3,k4)=(0.04,−0.01,0.002,−0.0003)(k_{1},k_{2},k_{3},k_{4})=(0.04,-0.01,0.002,-0.0003) for KB4, ξ=0.25\xi=0.25 and α=0.55\alpha=0.55 for Double-Sphere, α=0.55\alpha=0.55 and β=1\beta=1 for EUCM, and a vertical field of view of 90∘90^{\circ} for ERP-Crop and Cylindrical.

Figure 10: One checkpoint with and without the ray map. Ray map is the true ray field and Fallback is the equirectangular one the backbone assumes when none is supplied. Colour is distance to the ground truth as a fraction of the scene radius, on the scale of Fig. 9. Every camera degrades when the ray map is withdrawn except the equirectangular one in the last row, where the fallback coincides with the true field and nothing changes.

Figure 11: The eight central camera models. The same 360∘360^{\circ} panorama imaged through each lens, so every difference in distortion and in coverage comes from the camera model alone. Under each panel: field of view, then the fraction of the sphere that lens observes. Overlaid graticule: equator in red, prime meridian in teal, 45∘45^{\circ} meridians and 30∘30^{\circ} parallels in white, and the region outside the image circle in light grey.

Figure 12: From one panorama to a native camera frame. Top: the source panorama with the footprints of a 90∘90^{\circ} pinhole and a 200∘200^{\circ} fisheye marked. Middle: the ray map with direction shown as colour, the validity mask, and the resampled image. Bottom: the same panorama through all eight models. A fresh camera is drawn per view during training.

Figure 13: Acc against field of view, each method normalised by its own 90∘90^{\circ} value and averaged over the three datasets. The left panel shows all seven general-purpose methods and the right one Any3R and the three that degrade least, on a magnified scale. Below one means the wider lens is the easier one for that method.

Figure 14: Real pinhole imagery on three DL3DV scenes with three views each. Every method fuses its own per-view points with its own predicted poses, one similarity transform fitted on the tracks of the released structure-from-motion reconstruction places each cloud, and each row is rendered from one viewpoint. Sky pixels are found once per input image and removed from every method, and each cloud drops its own farthest 10%10\% of points from its own cameras.

Figure 15: One camera per row, one crop per column, on Matterport3D. The inset in each cell is the input that produced it, and the pair of numbers is its Acc and the field of view left after cropping. The viewpoint is shared along a row, so a row shows the field of view narrowing and the reconstruction shrinking together.

Figure 16: Accuracy against field of view with the camera held fixed. Each input is centre-cropped to 1.001.00, 0.750.75, 0.500.50, 0.350.35 and 0.200.20 of its width and resized back, so only the field of view changes. Reading a curve right to left is reading what a narrower lens costs.

Figure 17: Convergence of an earlier full run. Forty epochs from the original initialisation on eight A100s, evaluated under the paper protocol at 518×1036518{\times}1036 on equirectangular input. Dashed lines give the released panoramic baseline on the same protocol; the shaded band is the warm-up.
